title: Most Arguments Are Just Confident Guessing
author: What Teachers Have to Say
source: What Teachers Have to Say (whatteachershavetosay.substack.com), August 12, 2026
summary: A teacher-writer at the What Teachers Have to Say newsletter describes "Claim Jumper," an EduProtocol classroom routine built on a Gold Rush metaphor: readers who accept an argument's conclusion without checking its evidence are "claim jumpers" who take a strike someone else never actually proved. The routine has students extract a claim from a text -- a Yelp review, an ad, a speech -- into the center of a four-square Frayer-style chart, then fill the surrounding quadrants with evidence, effect, secondary evidence, and counterargument before sorting claims by strength at an "Assay Office" and synthesizing a final "Get Rich" analysis. The author walks through two worked examples, a three-star Yelp review and the O2 "Be More Dog" ad, to show the protocol exposing unsupported claims and contrast-driven persuasion, and then describes a "reverse move" that repurposes the same four-box structure as a pre-writing tool so students assay their own arguments before submitting them. The piece closes with several run-time variations (small-group jigsaw, pass-along analysis, multi-day sequencing) and a caution that students need scaffolded practice before running the routine independently.
points: Claim Jumper's core move is forcing students to locate a text's real claim and test it against four boxes -- evidence, effect, secondary evidence, counterargument -- rather than accepting confidently stated assertions as self-evidently true.

Applied to a three-star Yelp review, the protocol surfaced that the reviewer's actual argument ("the drive and parking ruin an otherwise great experience") was never supported with evidence, exposing a pattern the author says mirrors most everyday argumentation students encounter.
Run in reverse, the same four-quadrant structure becomes a pre-writing tool, letting students assay the strength of their own thesis and evidence before a teacher ever grades the draft.
The protocol is designed to run in as little as 20 minutes a week once established, prioritizing frequent, low-prep repetition over occasional deep-dive rhetorical analysis units.
quotes: But, this summer, a room full of teachers at the EduProtocols Summer Academy read her review together, sitting in the very city she was rating, and we noticed something usable: nothing in it was backed by evidence. Claims stacked on claims, no support in sight.

A jumper doesn't test the ground. He doesn't file paperwork or prove the strike is real. He just takes the claim once someone else has done that work and made it look valuable. That's what a reader does with an unexamined argument.

With Tishie's review, the room landed on her real argument fast. The three-star rating only makes sense if access is dragging down an otherwise positive experience. "The drive and parking ruin an otherwise great experience" is the claim doing most of the work, and she never supports it.

The room's verdict matched what my tenth graders once concluded: the ad works because everyone knows what boredom feels like and everyone wants to feel excited, so the argument runs on contrast rather than evidence.
By running the same four questions in reverse, students start assaying their own writing before anyone else has to grade it.
One caution from experience: students may need help discerning the claims at first. Calibrate as a class before diving deep, and start with something small. Move from success to success.
